sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
Historical earthquakes that have occurred on or along coastal areas are not infrequent in any country; the long Italian peninsula (and its large islands of Sardinia and Sicily) encircled by the Mediterranean Sea, is of course no exception (see data in Guidoboni and Ebel, 2009). After all, Italy has one of the longest historical seismicity records available, dating as back as the Vth century B.C. - thus allowing for more than one such "on-the-shore" earthquake to fall in the records.
Along-shore earthquakes can be often puzzling, for instance concerning their exact location -and, hence, their magnitude estimate, which is based on the automated treatment of the available macroseismic data (Bakun and Wentworth, 1997; Gasperini et al., 1999). To begin with, did such an earthquake really occur "on-the-shore"? Or is lack of historical information (especially for pre-instrumental era events) the main bias forcing seismicity catalogs to unavoidably place an epicenter just along the shore? Despite recent major improvements in the procedures that determine epicentral locations (Pasolini et al., 2008a & b; Gasperini et al., 2010), the circumstance of an along-shore location can affect earthquakes that took place in diverse areas and geodynamic contexts, giving room to a number of seismotectonic hypotheses -sometimes potentially biased due to a dubious epicentral location. Therefore, a) "deciding" whether an earthquake conceivably has occurred onshore or offshore on the basis of newly-available tectonic data and on further macroseismic considerations, b) understanding the kinematics of the potential seismogenic source of such earthquake and its recurrence time, and all the more c) weighting whether and how such event should be considered to assess seismic threat in a given area of suspected occurrence, can be of no little relevance.
Among some earthquakes that are reported in the current Italian macroseismic (Guidoboni et al., 2007) and parametric historical catalogs (Rovida et al., 2011), here we present the case of a relatively overlooked earthquake (Mw 5.4) that took place on 10 August 1893 and hit the Gargano peninsula, in the northeastern sector of the Puglia region (Molin, 1985). Although its location is on the coast, this event is but one of the several intermediate earthquakes that hit this region in the past few centuries and years (Suhadolc et al., 1983; Gasparini et al., 1985; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Camassi et al., 2008). Instrumental data are of course not available for the 1893 event, but the contemporary account by Grablovitz (1894), the reasonings by Baratta (1901) and space and time evidence provided by the historical catalogs allowed Fracassi et al. (2012) to show that a sequence of events have covered a 15-years time-lapse, all interestingly located along the Mattinata Fault Zone. The latter is a long-lived structure, well studied in the past from the tectonics (Bertotti et al., 1999; Chilovi et al., 2000; Billi et al., 2007), structural geology (Guerricchio et al., 1986; Funiciello et al., 1988; Salvini et al., 1999) and paleoseismology viewpoints (Piccardi, 2005; Tondi et al., 2005).
The Gondola Fault Zone (or System, or Ridge, auct.) has been long known to be a key tectonic feature just offshore the Gargano peninsula (De' Dominicis and Mazzoldi, 1987; Colantoni et al., 1990; de Alteriis and Aiello, 1993; Argnani et al., 1993; de Alteriis, 1995; Tramontana et al., 1995) and its complexities have been fathomed as deep as older seismic reflection data have allowed (for a good synthesis, see Morelli, 2002 and references therein).
Very-High-Resolution Chirp-sonar data have allowed Ridente et al. (2008) to study and analyze the brittle and ductile deformation of the Late Pleistocene-Holocene stratigraphy on top of the Gondola Fault Zone, at least concerning its ca. 50 km long, E-W main trend, just offshore the Gargano promontory. These authors recognized a number of structural elements and identified three fault segments. An in-depth analysis of its deformation and slip rates has then been tackled by Di Bucci et al. (2009) to constrain the time-frame of activity of the three segments, to then explore their seismogenic potential -the western one in particular. Fracassi et al. (2012) have eventually reassessed a number of cases of "just along the shore" earthquakes that have affected diverse aras of the Italian coastlines, to show that earthquake locations such as that of the 10 August 1893 Gargano earthquake might be misleading -and its magnitude estimate too. Also, data by Palombo et al. (2009) have unveiled offshore earthquakes (Mw ca. 5.5) located well offshore the Mattinata Fault and previously unknown to the catalogs, thus leading Fracassi et al. (2012) to strengthen the point that earthquakes with 'along the coast', dubious epicentral locations may lead to reconsider such earthquakes altogether, as shown by some inconsistencies among those few cases when both instrumental and macroseismic locations are available.
Size, strike, dip, rake, depth range, slip rate, and expected Mw of this Source are based on the geological data and seismological interpretations from Di Bucci et al. (2009) and from Fracassi et al. (2012).
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Did the 10 August 1893 earthquake really occur 15-20 km offshore E of Mattinata, the current location provided (at the time of writing) by the official parametric catalog? Was its magnitude therefore really underestimated? And, on a more provocative line of reasoning, could this be the only such case of biased location and magnitude of a coastal earthquake?
2) Could the recognized structure truly be a potential seismogenic source, if not yet activated - thus not responsible for the 1893 event? If so, which fault caused the 10 August 1893 earthquake? Was it inland, in the Gargano peninsula?
3) On the other hand, if this Source did cause the 1893 earthquake as Fracassi et al. (2012) maintain, is the longer (and larger) structure, adjacent to the east, a potential seismogenic source? If so, given the commonly accepted fault scaling laws, would this call for a potential seismic gap with Mw up to 6.5?
sections.SUMMARIES:
A number of workers have addressed the tectonic role of the inherited Gondola Fault Zone in the past. However, no specific studies had sought a seismogenic source for the 10 August 1893, nor suspected the possibility that such event might have occurred off-shore - although the contemporary accounts reported interesting hypotheses with this regard. Also, the degree of activity of some sectors of the Gondola Fault Zone has been recently at the center of scientific dispute, due in part to: 1) its juxtaposition to the Mattinata Fault just onshore, an area positively identified as the locus of historical and paleoseismological earthquakes - and also demonstrably active, given the 4.0 < Mw < ca. 5.0 instrumental events, and: 2) the interpretations of the recently available VHR and multi-channel seismic data.
Therefore, this Individual Source is mainly based upon data from Ridente et al. (2008), Di Bucci et al. (2009), and Fracassi et al. (2012).
Baratta (1894)
This contemporary scholar has reported a number of anomalies offshore that immediately preceded and fllowed the 10 August 1893 earthquake. Such phenomena included 'boiling water', 'flames at sea' reported by fishermen, 'whirling water' in a 5-km radius offshore the port of Mattinata, and mooring damages in the port itself.
Argnani et al. (1993)
These authors are among the first ones to provide an outlook of the deformation pattern in the Southern Adriatic Sea. They studied the South Gargano Deformation Belt, according to them formed between the Eocene and Early Pliocene times. They maintain this belt results as the Tertiary inversion of Mesozoic extensional faults.
Di Bucci et al. (2006)
These authors conducted a number of analogue sandbox models to reproduce a simplified, long fault system that includes the seismogenic sources of the 31 October-1 November Molise 2002 twin earthquakes (both Mw 5.8), the source of 30 July 1627 (Mw 6.7) Gargano earthquake, the Mattinata Fault and its ideal offshore prolongation (the Gondola Fault zone), identifying such system as the "Molise-Gondola shear zone". They hypothesize that such system, although highly fragmented, responds similarly along its 100+ km length to the present-day stress field that shows right-lateral, oblique strike-slip motion.
Ridente et al. (2008)
These authors present new Chirp Very High resolution seismic data to show the subtleties of the tectonic pattern overlying the shelf portion of the Gondola Fault. Mapping the various pieces of evidence shown on the Chirp cross-sections, their data and analyses show that the Gondola Fault is active and depict another view concerning the present-day tectonic framework in the eastern offshore of the Mattinata Fault.
Argnani et al. (2009)
These authors have concentrated on the Mattinata Fault and its offshore extent, including the Gondola Ridge, using new multi-channel seismic profiles and wells. They write that compression affected this system from the late Miocene to the Quaternary, with a limited strike-slip component. Based on the distribution of seismicity, they maintain that the offshore of the Mattinata Fault may not be the area undergoing present-day deformation.
Di Bucci et al. (2009)
These authors analyze new Chirp Very High resolution seismic data to reason on the actual degree of activity of some sectors of the Gondola Fault system in the first 50 km offshore the Mattinata Fault. They calculate deformation intervals and rates, slip rates on the various segments and hypothesize that the westernmost one could hold seismogenic potential.
Fracassi et al. (2012)
These authors reconsider a number of macroseismic data from four earthquakes that hit the Italian coast, in widely different contexts, and show some interesting traits of the seismic sequence that culminated with the 1893 earthquake -and that was followed by a number of events west of the port of Mattinata, i.e. along the Mattinata Fault. They then resume geological and structural data from previous work and devised a potential seismogenic source for the 1893 earthquake.

pictures.c: Three examples of moderate-sized earthquakes that have occurred along the Italian coastlines within the last 150 years. These include events such as the 10 August 1893 Mattinata one (the case-study here), for which only macroseismic information can be found, but also very recent cases like the 6 September 2002 Palermo earthquake, which was well covered by instrumental data (from Fracassi et al. [2012]).

Seismo-tectonic synthesis of south-eastern Italy and the adjacent southern Adriatic basin. The key elements are indeed the Apennines outer front, the seismogenic sources along the backbone of the southern Apennines (with extensional kinematics), those affecting the Apulian domain (witnessing deeper and oblique, right-lateral extension) and the inherited Gondola fault zone (from Fracassi et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Structural map of the Gondola Fault Zone (Ridente et al. [2008])
pictures.c: Structural map of the Gondola Fault Zone. The fault system is made up of a northern and a southern fault set. In the northern one three segments have been recognized (western central and eastern)

pictures.t: Example of Chirp-sonar seismic profiles across the Gondola Fault Zone
pictures.c: Three Chirp-sonar seismic profiles (tracks can be noticed in the previous figure) showing the structural style of the Gondola West Source (from Fracassi et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Distribution of displacement along the Gondola Fault Zone
pictures.c: Slip distribution in the northern and southern fault sets of the Gondola Fault Zone (from Di Bucci et al. [2009]). The fault system in its entirety shows a bell-shape displacement distribution along strike, with the largest throw recorded in the central segment of the northern set (which is also the longest). Diagram C well shows the activity and the displacement distribution for the western segment, which displaces both 20-30 ka and 5.5 ka reflectors.
Time-and-space distribution of the earthquake sequence that includes the 10 August 1893 Mattinata earthquake (from Fracassi et al. [2012]).
Limits that affect the Mw estimates for earthquake that have occurred along the coastline (or just offshore) predating the instrumental era (from Fracassi et al. [2012]).
